content.title: Artemis 2 Splashdown: NASA hails Orion astronauts' return from moon
content.text: Refresh April 11, 2026 at 4:07 AM NASA hails Orion astronauts' return from moon NASA’s Orion spacecraft is seen as recovery teams work to secure the spacecraft ahead of transferring Artemis 2 crewmembers. (Image credit: NASA/Joel Kowsky) NASA's post-splashdown press briefing has ended and I think it's safe to say that the space agency is over the moon at the amazing success of its Artemis 2 moon mission. All four Artemis 2 astronauts are in good health and will return home to NASA's Johnson Space Center on Saturday, April 11, one day after their smooth splashdown in the Pacific Ocean."Welcome to our moonshot," Lori Glaze, NASA's Artemis program manager, told reporters during a triumphant televised press briefing at the Johnson Space Center in Houston. Howard Hu, Orion spacecraft program manager, said the mission was "thousands of times better" than Star Wars, given its role as the vanguard of NASA's return to the moon.During reentry, NASA lost contact with the Orion spacecraft for six minutes due to plasma interference around the spacecraft. It was an expected comms dropout, but still, nerves were high."Certainly, there's anxiety," Artemis 2 entry flight director Rick Henflig said. "If you didn't have anxiety bringing the spacecraft home, you probably didn't have a pulse."But he and his team had extreme confidence in Orion's heat shield and performance, as did the rest of Mission Control and the astronauts themselves."And so while there's anxiety, there's a lot of confidence, because the team is there to do a job, and we've trained well and and we executed well. We all breathed a sigh of relief once the side hatch opened up," he added.NASA Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya said the success of Artemis 2 sets the stage for something greater, beyond Artemis 3, at the moon."The path to the lunar surface is open, but the work ahead is greater than the work behind us. It always will be," he said. "53 years ago, humanity left the moon. This time we return to stay.""Let us finish what they started. Let us focus on what was left undone. Let us not go to plant flags and leave, but to stay with firmness in our purpose, with gratitude for the hands who built the machines, and with love for the ones that we carry with us. Welcome home, Integrity." NASA chief Jared Isaacman greeted the four Artemis 2 astronauts with hugs and smiles after their return."Honestly, I'm still at a loss for words," Isaacman said from the deck of the USS John P. Muthra after splashdown. "The childhood Jared, right now, can't believe what I just saw. I mean almost been waiting my whole lifetime to see to see this, and then it's as NASA administrator, I just couldn't be more proud of the entire workforce, the years, the effort, the late nights, all the hard work from across the country that contributed to this incredible moment right now."With that, our live blog for Artemis 2 is at its end. Thank you, Space Fans, for coming along with us on this mission over the last few months (and years, if you were following on the site).The entire Space.com team worked together to bring you our coverage. So a huge shout out to Brett Tingley, Mike Wall, Josh Dinner, Monisha Ravisetti and Daisy Dobrijevic for the mission updates on this page, to Steve Spaleta (who brought you all the video), Vanessa Jewell on our Socials and our Content Manager Chelsea Gohd for awesome images. And to the rest of our team, Ian Stokes, Anthony Wood, Rob Lea, Jase Parnell-Brookes and Harry Bennett for their amazing stories.Now our eyes turn to Artemis 3, and hopefully a moon landing in 2028 with Artemis 4. We'll see you then, Space Fans!Keep looking up. April 11, 2026 at 2:27 AM Artemis 2 splashdown success: NASA briefing at 10:30 pm ET (Image credit: NASA/Bill Ingalls) It has now been just over 2 hours since the successful splashdown of NASA's Artemis 2 astronauts at 8:07 p.m. EDT and all four astronauts are safely aboard the USS John P. Murtha recovery ship and undergoing medical checks.NASA's live webcast has ended, but a press conference will begin at 10:30 p.m. EDT (0230 GMT), so in a few minutes. You'll be able to watch it here. April 11, 2026 at 2:17 AM Artemis 2 astronauts get warm welcome on recovery ship Artemis 2 astronaut Christina Koch waves on her way to the recovery ship medical bay. (Image credit: NASA) The four Artemis 2 astronauts are getting a warm welcome aboard the USS John P. Murtha as they head to medical checks. NASA Chief Jared Isaacman met each crewmember, sharing hugs and congratulatory words with each."Welcome, Integrity," an announcement rang out. Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen was the first to walk from his helicopter to the medical bay, waving with a broad smile.NASA mission specialist Christina Koch was next, waving excitedly and smiling.Pilot Victor Glover, a Navy Captain, wore a ship's hat, waved and saluted as he walked across the flight deck.Commander Reid Wiseman also waved and gave a thumbs up as we walked to the medical bay.All four astronauts walked under their own power, though ship officials had prepared wheelchairs in case they were needed. They were not. April 11, 2026 at 1:57 AM All Artemis 2 astronauts recovered by helicopters On the ship, a bell was rung and announcement rang out."Integrity, arriving." April 11, 2026 at 1:53 AM Helicopters begin picking up Artemis 2 astronauts (Image credit: NASA) Helicopters are now retrieving each of the four Artemis 2 crewmembers.Each astronaut is wearing a special harness to be hoisted up to a helicopter along with a recovery specialist. Two astronauts have been recovred by different helicopters so far. April 11, 2026 at 1:41 AM Artemis 2 astronauts exit Orion spacecraft after splashdown (Image credit: NASA) All four Artemis 2 astronauts have exited their Orion spacecraft, their home to the moon and back for the last 10 days after today's successful splashdown.Artemis 2 commander Reid Wiseman was the last crewmember to leave the Orion spacecraft Integrity. They are sitting on a floating inflatable "front porch" and awaiting basket retrieval by helictoper. Two helicopters will recover two astroanuts each to transport them to the nearby USS John P. Murtha recovery ship.Here's a video replay of splashdown if you missed it at 8:07 p.m. EDT. April 11, 2026 at 1:22 AM All 4 Artemis 2 astronauts 'feeling great' Small boats travel to the Orion capsule as part of Artemis 2 recovery efforts. (Image credit: NASA/Joel Kowsky) NASA's Megan Cruz reports that the undersea medical officer inside the Orion spacecraft has completed initial health checks of the four Artemis 2 astronauts."All four Artemis 2 crewmembers are feeling great" Cruz said. The recovery divers are inflating a stabilization collar around the base of the Orion capsule. Strong ocean currents have slowed their efforts, but progress is being made.The recovery tean has clearly inflated a large "front porch" platform and will soon attach it to the front of Orion. April 11, 2026 at 1:02 AM Side hatch of Orion capsule opened by recovery team (Image credit: NASA) Recovery teams have reached the Orion spacecraft and the side hatch is open, NASA reports.Four recovery teammembers will enter Orion to check the status of the four Artemis 2 astronauts. A total of 40 people are in boats around Orion to aid in recovery efforts. One group is attaching a "front porch" inflatable platform to extract the crew onto. Two helicopters will then come to carry the cre back to the USS John P. Murtha recovery ship. Two crewmembers will fly on each helicopter. April 11, 2026 at 12:48 AM Orion spacecraft Integrity powered down after splashdown (Image credit: NASA) Good night, Integrity and thank you. Artemis 2 commander Reid Wiseman reports the vehicle is now fully powered down.NASA and U.S. Navy recovery teams are en route to the Artemis 2 Orion spacecraft Integrity. They will attach an inflatable "front porch" to the capsule near the hatch, where the crew will be extracted to so they can be ferried to the waiting USS John P. Murtha recovery ship for medical checks. Orion will be towed to the ship's well deck for recovery.NASA has also issued a new exact splashdown time of 8:07:27 p.m. EDT (0007:27 GMT), for a total mission elapsed time of 9 days, 1 hour, 32 minutes and 15 seconds. April 11, 2026 at 12:31 AM NASA Administrator Isaacman offers remarks from recovery ship Orion will splashdown at a speed of 17 mph. (Image credit: NASA) HOUSTON — NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, aboard Orion's recovery ship, gave remarks after the crew's splashdown."Honestly, I'm still at a loss for words," he said. "The childhood, Jared, right now, can't believe what I just saw. I've almost been waiting my whole lifetime to see this, and then, as NASA administrator, I just couldn't be more proud of the entire workforce — the years, the effort, the late nights, all the hard work from across the country that contributed to this incredible moment right now." April 11, 2026 at 12:09 AM Splashdown confirmed! HOUSTON — Splashdown! Orion will splashdown at a speed of 17 mph. (Image credit: NASA) April 11, 2026 at 12:06 AM Main chutes delpoyed! Orion will splashdown at a speed of 17 mph. (Image credit: NASA) HOUSTON — Orion has successfully deployed its main parachutes. April 11, 2026 at 12:04 AM Orion successfully deploys drogue parachutes During its plunge, Orion will reach a maximum speed of 24,661 mph (39688 kph). (Image credit: NASA) Drogues deployed! HOUSTON — Orion has successfully deployed its first set of parachutes, the drogues, designed to slow the spacecraft in preparation for the main parachutes.In one minute, Orion will deploy its main parachutes. April 11, 2026 at 12:01 AM NASA reestablishes contact with Orion During its plunge, Orion will reach a maximum speed of 24,661 mph (39688 kph). (Image credit: NASA) Hello again, Orion! HOUSTON — NASA has reestablished communications with Orion, after a 6-minute blackout as the spacecraft made its way through Earth's upper atmosphere.Now in free fall, Orion's speed will continue to slow, leading up to the deployment of the capsules drogue parachutes, and then its main chutes, which will ultimately slow the vehicle to its splashdown velocity. The two drogue parachutes will deploy at 8:03 p.m. EDT (0003 GMT, April 11), at an altitude of about 22,000 feet (6,705 m), and slow Orion to about 300 mph (482 kph).The main chutes will deploy a minute later, at 8:04 p.m. EDT (0004 GMT, April 11)k, at about 6,000 feet (1,828 m). April 10, 2026 at 11:54 PM Orion has officially encountered Earth's atmosphere, enters comms blackout During its plunge, Orion will reach a maximum speed of 24,661 mph (39688 kph). (Image credit: NASA) Things are moving fast now — even though Orion is slowing down. HOUSTON — Orion has hit the atmosphere! The Artemis 2 crew officially entered the Earth's atmosphere at 7:53 p.m. EDT (2353 GMT). Now, as the spacecraft rapidly slows from a breakneck 24,661 mph (39688 kph) — Mach 33 — the capsule will be engulfed in a sheet of plasma. April 10, 2026 at 11:35 PM Successful separation from Orion's European Service Module Orion's European Service Module is the white cylindrical section of the spacecraft, which has provided power and life support during their mission. (Image credit: NASA) Farewell, European Service Module! HOUSTON — Orion has officially shed its service module. The European Space Agency- built spacecraft stage has powered and supplied the Integrity capsule since launch, providing propellant, water, air and solar arrays used to power Orion during its trip to the moon. Separation occurred at 7:33 p.m. EDT (2333 GMT)."Houston we got a great view of the European Service module out the window with the sun hitting the side and the solar arrays and the NASA worm right there. It's a beautiful looking machine," NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman said. After separating from the service module, Orion will perform a "Crew Module Raise Burn." to put some distance between the two spacecraft sections. The service module will then begin its own plunge toward Earth, and is expected to burn up in the atmosphere.Orion will officially hit Earth's atmosphere at approximately 7:53 p.m. EDT (2353 GMT), at which point the spacecraft will enter a 6-minute communications blackout, expected to last until 7:59 p.m. EDT (2359 GMT). April 10, 2026 at 11:16 PM Orion switches communications off Deep Space Network, weather is "go" The 70-meter antenna at the Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex in the Mohave Desert in California. (Image credit: NASA/JPL) They are officially close to home. HOUSTON — As Orion continues to close the gap between the spacecraft and Earth, NASA has switched its comms source from the Deep Space Network to the Telemetry and Data Relay Satellite System, or TDRSS, in Earth orbit to maintain communications.The weather forecast has been given a "go" from the Spaceflight Meteorology group at NASA's Johnson Space Center. At 7:33 p.m. EDT (2333 GMT), Orion will separate from its service module, which has maintained the majority of the spacecraft's systems over the past nine days. April 10, 2026 at 10:27 PM NASA's live coverage of Orion's return begins (Image credit: NASA) The astronauts are putting on their spacesuits and orienting Orion for return HOUSTON — The Artemis 2 astronauts are putting on their spacesuits and are gearing up for for return to Earth. Currently, they are going through their pre-entry checklist, and making sure everything is buttoned down before the hit the atmosphere.As they prepare, the Earth in NASA's livestream is quickly growing larger as Orion brings the Artemis 2 astronauts closer to home. — on NASA's landing coverage will officially begin at 6:30 p.m. EDT (2230 GMT), and will be carried on Space.com's homepage, this live updates pages and on our homepage and our VideoFromSpace YouTube channel.Today is splashdown day for Artemis 2 moon astronauts — What to expect at each stage of reentry & landing (timeline) April 10, 2026 at 7:36 PM Splashdown Day: Artemis 2 astronauts complete Orion's final trajectory correction burn (Image credit: NASA) Earth is getting bigger outside Orion's window. HOUSTON — It's a busy day here at NASA's Johnson Space Center, with all eyes on Orion as it approaches reentry.Orion recently completed its third and final trajectory correction burn, which has put them on course for a precise splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, about 60 miles (100 kilometers) off the coast of San Diego. Continued below... — on Now, the crew continues their preparations for return, soon donning their spacesuits to strap in for atmospheric reentry. We'll be tracking as Orion continues on its approach, which you can watch live on Space.com starting at 6:30 p.m. EDT (2230 GMT).Today is splashdown day for Artemis 2 moon astronauts — What to expect at each stage of reentry & landing (timeline) April 10, 2026 at 3:53 PM Splashdown Day: Artemis 2 astronauts start running to the water Here are some of the lyrics:In a moment we lost our minds hereAnd lay our spirit downToday we lived a thousand yearsAll we have is nowRun to the waterAnd find me thereBurnt to the core but not brokenWe'll cut through the madnessOf these streets below the moonThese streets below the moonAnd, as a sort of bonus song this morning, the crew also got to hear a snippet of "Free" by Zac Brown Band. This one was technically not a wakeup song per se, as it was the start of the typical message that follows these songs: This time from Zac Brown Band itself.As for crew activities today, it's all about a safe splashdown. "Can't wait to see you run to the water, see you soon," Mission Control said to the astronauts after they woke up.You can see a full list of the crew's wakeup songs here and, if you want to relive the experience even after the mission is over, here's out Spotify playlist of the tracks. — on April 10, 2026 at 1:56 PM SPLASHDOWN DAY: Less than 70,000 miles to go! (Image credit: Future) NASA's Artemis 2 crew is now within 70,000 miles of Earth as Orion continues its journey home ahead of tonight's splashdown.As Orion makes its approach, Earth appears as a crescent, a bright curve of blue and white that almost looks like a smile welcoming them home. The astronauts will wake up at 11:35 a.m. EDT (1535 GMT) before carrying out a final trajectory correction burn at 2:53 p.m. EDT (1853) to fine-tune their path back to Earth.After 10 days around the moon and back, the final approach is well underway. (Image credit: NASA) As NASA's Orion spacecraft makes its way back to Earth, all eyes are on the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of California, where splashdown is expected tonight.But why this location? How is it chosen? Check out our full landing schedule for everything you need to know.We'll be following all the action live right here, so stay tuned! April 10, 2026 at 10:07 AM SPLASHDOWN DAY: Artemis 2 returns to Earth TODAY! NASA's Orion spacecraft shortly after the Artemis 1 mission, Dec. 11, 2022. (Image credit: NASA) Happy landing day! Who's excited?!Today (April 10), NASA's Artemis 2 astronauts will return to Earth, wrapping up their historic 10-day journey to the moon and back. What a journey it has been!Live coverage of the splashdown begins at 6:30 p.m. EDT (2230 GMT) here on Space.com, with splashdown currently expected for approximately 8:07 p.m. EDT (0007 GMT).If you've been glued to the mission livestreams and our live blog over the past 10 days as we have, you might be wondering what to do with all that free time once it's over... but we're not quite there yet. There is still a full day of Artemis 2 action ahead.We'll be updating the live blog throughout the day with the latest developments, so stick with us as we follow every moment of Artemis 2's return to Earth. April 10, 2026 at 1:38 AM Flight Day 9: Artemis 2 astronauts are halfway homeThey've hit the midway point between Earth and the moon (Image credit: NASA) The Artemis 2 astronauts have hit the midway point in their journey back to Earth from the moon, according to NASA.The quartet — NASA's Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover Christina Koch and the Canadian Space Agency's Jeremy Hansen — remain on track arrive at their home planet on Friday evening (April 10). If all goes according to plan, they'll hit Earth's atmosphere over the open Pacific Ocean at 7:53 p.m. EDT (2353 GMT) and splash down off the coast of San Diego 14 minutes later. You can watch their homecoming live, and get other updates about their historic mission, here at Space.com. April 9, 2026 at 8:21 PM Flight Day 9: NASA gearing up for Artemis 2 astronauts' return"The crew has done their part. Now we have to do ours." Artemis 2 astronauts aboard Orion. (Image credit: NASA) HOUSTON — As Orion picks ups speed on its journey back from the moon, NASA officials say its time for the work of mission engineers and technicians to be put on full display."To every engineer, every technician that's touched this machine tomorrow belongs to you," said NASA Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya, during a mission update briefing today (April 9). "The crew has done their part. Now we have to do ours." The Artemis 2 astronauts return to Earth tomorrow, and face one of the most risky parts of their mission.Orion's return trajectory plan for Artemis 2 was altered after the heat shield on Artemis 1 experienced unexpected char and material losses during atmospheric reentry. Now, rather than hitting the atmosphere head-one, Orion will perform what's called a "lofted" reentry, dipping down into the atmosphere briefly, before delving back down for its final descent — similar to a stone skipping once across a pond before sinking beneath the water.The flight path is designed to reduce heat stress on Orion's heatshield, decelerating the spacecraft in separate increments to better distribute its building energy, but the risk isn't entirely mitigated."Let's not beat around the bush," said Artemis 2 lead flight director Jeff Radigan during Thursday's briefing. "We have to hit that angle correctly, otherwise we're not going to have a successful entry,"Orion will begin its plunge through the atmosphere on Friday (April 10) at around 7:53 p.m. EDT (2353 GMT), entering a 6-minute communications blackout. The spacecraft's two parachute groups, its drogues and the main chutes, will deploy around 8:03 p.m. EDT (0003 GMT, April 11) and 8:04 p.m. EDT (0004 GMT, April 11), respectively, with splashdown expected at 8:07 p.m. EDT (0007 GMT, April 11). 'It just made it even more special': Being so far from Earth makes you appreciate our planet even more, Artemis 2 astronaut says April 9, 2026 at 4:06 PM Flight Day 9: Artemis 2 astronauts wake up to 'Lonesome Drifter' The Artemis 2 astronauts were woken up on Thursday (April 9) morning to the song "Lonesome Drifter" by Charley Crockett — though the world would argue these adventurers are anything but. They even named a crater after commander Reid Wiseman's late wife who passed away from cancer in 2020.Today's activities, according to Mission Control, mostly surround preparing for splashdown tomorrow.And, of course, if you're interested in the rest of the crew's wakeup songs — and are curious what they'll be listening to during reentry — you can have a look at our Spotify playlist here. April 9, 2026 at 2:24 PM Flight Day 9: Artemis 2 Astronauts enter their final full day in spaceToday is all about packing for the final leg home. Artemis 2 astronauts post aboard Orion for a selfie. (Image credit: NASA) HOUSTON — Good morning from NASA's Johnson Space Center, and the final full day of the Artemis 2 mission. Flight Day 9 of the astronauts' mission aboard Orion will primarily focus on packing and stowing everything aboard their spacecraft in preparation for their return to Earth.Yesterday, the Artemis 2 crew had the opportunity to speak with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, and took some time last night to answer some questions from the media, though Space.com was, unfortunately, not called on to pose a query of our own. BUT THAT'S OK! I held a miniature interview of my own, and was still able to take a little time to ask a few short questions... Space.com spaceflight staff writer Josh Dinner asks the Artemis 2 astronaut cutout figures a few questions. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) Crew wakeup is scheduled today (April 9) at 11:35 a.m. EDT (1535 GMT). They do have a few more demonstration tests to carry out today, practicing various procedures for a few off-nominal scenarios. They’ll also be donning and fitting compression clothes designed to help their bodies readjust to gravity after landing, which they also spent some time yesterday doing. Those are called orthostatic intolerant garments, and help to counteract symptoms like dizziness and lightheadedness after time spent in zero-g. By the end of today, the couches in Orion will be secured back in place, and the Artemis 2 crew will be fully ready for their return home, with the final leg of their mission just ahead. Tomorrow will bring an end to their mission, with a splashdown scheduled for tomorrow (April 10), at 8:07 p.m. EDT (0007 GMT, April 11). 'It just made it even more special': Being so far from Earth makes you appreciate our planet even more, Artemis 2 astronaut says April 9, 2026 at 3:44 AM Flight Day 8: Artemis 2 astronauts answer questions on the way home to EarthThe quartet talked about the highlights of their mission so far (Image credit: NASA) The Artemis 2 astronauts took some time out of their busy moon mission tonight (April 8) to answer a few questions from reporters.Those questions were pretty diverse. For example, Artemis 2 commander Reid Wiseman was asked how he felt when his crewmates proposed naming a moon crater after his late wife Carroll. "For me personally, that was kind of the pinnacle moment of the mission," Wiseman responded. "That was, I think, where the four of us were the most forged, the most bonded, and we came out of that really focused on that day ahead."Artemis 2 pilot Victor Glover cited witnessing a total solar eclipse from beyond the moon as one of his mission highlights. And mission specialist Christina Koch relayed what it's like to live inside the Orion capsule."We have loved living in Orion, and in fact, we've all said that sometimes you can forget where you really are, because we're in this small space that just gives us everything we need," she said.But, even though the capsule feels bigger in microgravity, "we are bumping into each other 100% of the time," she added. "A phrase that you often hear in the cabin is, 'Don't move your foot. I'm just going to reach for something right under it.'"Artemis 2 is in the home stretch of its 10-day mission; Orion will come back to Earth on Friday evening (April 10), splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego. April 8, 2026 at 10:34 PM Flight Day 8: Artemis 2 won't break Apollo's speed record after allBut everything remains on track for a safe return on April 10 (Image credit: NASA) Everything remains on track for Artemis 2's safe return to Earth on Friday evening (April 10). But there is a twist: It looks like the mission won't break the human spaceflight speed record after all.That mark is held by the Apollo 10 moon mission, which reached a maximum speed of 36,397 feet per second — 24,816 mph, or 39,938 kph — when it returned to Earth on May 26, 1969. We'd been told that Artemis 2 will top that mark, but the latest calculations have it coming up a bit short during its own reentry. "Our prediction for Artemis 2 — we're going to reach a max velocity of 34,965 feet per second," Artemis 2 Flight Director Rick Henfling said during a press conference this afternoon (April 8). That works out to 23,840 mph, or 38,367 kph.If all goes to plan, Artemis 2's Orion capsule will hit Earth's atmosphere at 7:53 p.m. EDT (2353 GMT) on Friday, then splash down 14 minutes later. It will come down in the Pacific Ocean off the San Diego coast; the four astronauts will then be recovered and brought ashore for medical evaluations. April 8, 2026 at 7:30 PM Flight Day 8: Astronauts begin stowing their gear for returnArtemis 2 astronauts have begun preparations for their return to Earth Artemis 2 astronauts post aboard Orion for a selfie. (Image credit: NASA) HOUSTON — The Artemis 2 astronauts aboard Orion are continuing their flight back from the moon, and have started wrapping up aspects of the mission to prepare for their plunge through Earth's atmosphere.NASA astronaut and Artemis 2 commander Reid Wiseman began his scheduled exercise routine today (April 8) at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT) — an activity each crew member has partaken in daily to stave off the effects of microgravity on their muscles and bones. Before his workout, however, Reid called down to mission control to confirm that this would be his last exercise routine before the crew's return April 10."Can you confirm this is my final exercise of the mission," Wiseman said to Mission Control. "It'll just help me with stowage management."The crew's final exercise is one of the milestones marking the final leg of their journey — and stowing everything aboard Orion, including the crew's flywheel exercise machine, is important. Loose gear can be dangerous during reentry.Artemis 2 is scheduled to splash down on April 10, at 8:07 p.m. EDT (0007 GMT, April 11). Before they do, though, Orion will break another spaceflight record when it hits Earth's atmosphere at 25,000 mph (40,230 kph), and that can be a bumpy ride. Any free-flying equipment aboard the spacecraft will become a hazard during that phase of flight, and securing heavy gear like exercise equipment is crucial.Later today, the astronauts will hold a live event with the Canadian Space Agency , practice radiation-shielding procedures and hold a short press conference at 9:45 p.m. EDT (0145 GMT on April 9).Tonight, the astronauts will perform maneuverability tests with Orion, switching between the spacecraft's two modes of attitude control. 'It just made it even more special': Being so far from Earth makes you appreciate our planet even more, Artemis 2 astronaut says April 8, 2026 at 4:02 PM Flight Day 8: Artemis 2 astronauts wake up to "Under Pressure"They also got a nice message from Canadian Space Agency employees Flight Day 8 of the Artemis 2 mission around the moon kicked off today (April 8) at 11:35 a.m. EDT (1335 GMT) with a great wakeup song — "Under Pressure" by David Bowie and Queen. (There was some drama when the first notes of that famous bassline hit, however: Were we hearing that classic or "Ice Ice Baby?")After shutting off the song, Mission Control beamed up a nice message from the Canadian Space Agency (CSA). "Good morning, Artemis 2!" a crowd of CSA workers hollered at the four astronauts. Then, a single voice delivered these words: "Your friends and colleagues at the Canadian Space Agency wish you another great day on your voyage. Canadians everywhere are inspired by your journey, and we're with you every step of the way. Let's go!"The CSA has an astronaut on Artemis 2, of course — mission specialist Jeremy Hansen. He's flying with four NASA astronauts: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch.Flight Day 8 will be a rather sedate one for the quartet, at least compared to the action-packed Flight Day 6, when they made their record-breaking flyby of the moon. The astronauts will hold a live CSA downlink event at 7:20 p.m. EDT (2320 GMT), conduct a radiation-shielding experiment an hour later, and talk to reporters at 9:45 p.m. EDT (0145 GMT on April 9). Then, at 10:59 p.m. EDT (0259 GMT), they'll do some manual flying with their Orion capsule to further test its capabilities.Artemis 2 launched on April 1 and is now in the home stretch of its historic journey. The mission will return to Earth on Friday evening (April 10), splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego. April 8, 2026 at 12:38 PM Flight Day 8: Astronauts cruise toward Earth during Flight Day 8Radiation and thruster control tests lie ahead HOUSTON — Good morning, all, and welcome to flight day 8 of the Artemis 2 mission!As they make their way back from the moon, the astronauts have a full day ahead of them. After their wakeup call, the Artemis 2 astronauts will practice in-flight procedures for dealing with incoming radiation, as well as tests on Orion's attitude control system modes. Radiation is a constant presence in space and can pose risks to both biology and technology. In the event of a major radiation event, like a solar flare, the astronauts take shelter inside Orion, barricading themselves between the spacecraft's heat shield and stacks of supplies that can absorb the brunt of the incoming particles.They'll also test out Orion's two attitude control system modes. The spacecraft has two thruster modes: six-degree-of-freedom and three-degree-of-freedom attitude controls. The six-degree configuration ensures Orion's course isn't altered as the spacecraft makes attitude adjustments, auto-correcting any deviation caused by the slight movements. In the three-degree configuration, Orion uses less fuel and requires less complex calculations, but requires course corrections due to inevitable drift. — on 'It just made it even more special': Being so far from Earth makes you appreciate our planet even more, Artemis 2 astronaut says April 8, 2026 at 3:35 AM Flight Day 7: Artemis 2's space toilet is working OK — but there's still a problemThe astronauts can't vent their urine properly Another day, another toilet update. On Tuesday (April 7), a day after Artemis 2's epic flyby of the moon, NASA officials gave us some more news about the mission's famous space toilet.The loo has had its issues during the mission, but we learned on Tuesday that it's actually working well now.
